desc: Police shot a loose wild cat, reported as a caracal though a police report called it a lynx.
title: Caracal shot by police, Fintona

desc: Two teachers watched a silent silver cone-shaped object about 100 m up for around five minutes before it vanished. A local monitor speculated about a spy plane.
title: Carlisle silver cone

desc: A slow-moving object was watched for about half an hour travelling east to west and repeatedly retracing its path; witnesses ruled out an aircraft. No explanation was given.
title: Carrickmacross retracing object

desc: The hotel is said to be haunted by an angry chambermaid whose last wish was ignored, and guests report a phantom cat climbing onto beds at night.
title: Castle Hotel chambermaid, Conwy

desc: Reports include a lady in green near the Dickens Bar and twin girls seen at the foot of beds.
place: Castle Mona, Douglas, Isle of Man
title: Castle Mona green lady

desc: The 14th-century castle, scene of many executions, has reports of shadowy figures, a White Lady and a Woman in Black.
place: Castle Rushen, Castletown, Isle of Man
title: Castle Rushen White Lady

desc: A Mr Thomas reportedly found a metallic object in the dunes and was warned off with 'powerful rays' by two men who said they had visited Earth for centuries. The date was not recorded beyond 1952; coordinates are for Castlemartin village.
source: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave

sources.name: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave

title: Castlemartin dunes metallic object and 'ray' men

desc: In 1997 a 'cat-like beast' was reported to have attacked a foal at Felingwm, near Carmarthen.

sources.name: Spooky Isles

title: Cat-like beast attacks foal at Felingwm

desc: Legend says Catherine Howard broke from her guards in 1541 and ran along the gallery to plead with Henry VIII; it has since been called the Haunted Gallery.
place: Haunted Gallery, Hampton Court Palace, London
title: Catherine Howard, Hampton Court

desc: After a crash at Fiveways while rushing his pregnant wife to hospital, a man woke to be told his wife and three children had never existed. Tom Slemen calls it one of his strangest cases; names were changed.

sources.name: Liverpool Echo

title: Childwall man whose family never existed

desc: Legend tells of a cave near the castle entrance that draws in anyone who comes within five paces. A fiddler who walked in playing one Halloween never came out, and a fox fled out smelling of brimstone.
title: Chirk Castle cave of no return

desc: Three ghosts, including a Civil War cavalier and the original owner's father, are said to haunt the 16th-century house, where objects move; it was investigated in 2007.
place: Churche's Mansion, Hospital Street, Nantwich, Cheshire
title: Churche's Mansion, Nantwich

desc: Two brothers visiting family saw a circular object heading towards the Berwyns, then a brighter, oddly flashing light over the far side of the lake that climbed quickly. A Llanuwchllyn family reported orange circular objects over the mountains.
title: Circular object and light over Llyn Tegid

desc: A large glassy sphere was watched over the coast for more than an hour and reportedly painted on radar at RAF Manby, departing as RAF aircraft approached. No explanation was given.
source: Wikipedia – UFO sightings in the United Kingdom
title: Cleethorpes glass sphere tracked by RAF Manby

desc: Two oval orbs were seen and photographed; conventional aircraft were said to have been ruled out. No identification was offered.
title: Clifden oval orbs photographed

desc: The Welsh Federation of Independent Ufologists recorded a cluster of UFO reports around the Clwydian Range, Prestatyn, Meliden and Dyserth in 1985 and 1986.

sources.name: Daily Post

title: Clwydian Range UFO flap

desc: A Victorian boy crushed by a coal delivery is said to haunt the mansion; staff describe sickness after taunting him and footsteps along a corridor at night. The cellar is now sealed.

sources.name: Liverpool Echo

title: Coal-cellar boy of Calderstones House

desc: Windows along the street were smashed by flying lumps of coal, and the breakages carried on even after police began patrolling.

sources.name: Paranormal Database

title: Coal-throwing outbreak, Myers Street

desc: A long-exposure photograph of the library taken in 1891, while Lord Combermere's funeral was under way, appears to show a figure in his chair.
title: Combermere Abbey ghost photo

desc: Two police officers reported a domed object about 100 ft across with lit portholes near the A629. No explanation was recorded.
source: Wikipedia – UFO sightings in the United Kingdom
title: Cononley police domed craft

desc: Coombs children (named as Keiran and Layanne in one account) reported three hovering UFOs, the lowest of which lowered a metal ladder down which a silver-clad figure climbed, leaving a bright red 'box' that could not afterwards be found. The children reportedly developed blotchy red patches on their skin the next day. Coordinates approximate (clifftop fields seaward of the farm).
place: Clifftop fields near Ripperston Farm, Pembrokeshire
source: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave

source: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave

desc: A huge arrowhead-shaped object, described as the size of ten football pitches, was reported. A local astronomer argued such sightings can usually be explained, but none was given for this case.
title: Corbridge giant arrowhead

desc: Owen Evans of Maesydderwen, Llansawel, told Ceredig Davies that in his boyhood a young man saw a light inside the locked Silian church. With Evans's father he watched it move and sink into the ground, and they marked the spot with a stick. A death followed and the person was buried on that spot.
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

sources.name: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg
Ceredigion History

title: Corpse candle sinks into Silian churchyard

desc: A patch of scrub next to Liverpool's oldest church is said to be protected by an old promise never to build on it. Tales describe coloured orbs ('corpse candles'), 'black goblins' and a dark figure that rises before wars.
place: Bloody Acre, All Saints Church, Childwall

sources.name: Liverpool Echo (Tom Slemen)

title: Corpse candles of Bloody Acre, Childwall

desc: A large triangular craft reported over RAF Cosford and RAF Shawbury. Investigated by the MoD's Nick Pope.
title: Cosford incident

desc: An angler photographed a humming metallic disc hovering over the reservoir for more than 15 minutes before it sped off. Checks with the RAF, airports and police found no known traffic.
title: Craigluscar Reservoir metallic disc

desc: An RAF pilot and student flying at 2,000 ft reported an object climbing to around 25,000 ft before appearing to explode. RAF and civil police investigated; no explanation was given.
source: The National Archives – UFO files highlights (March 2009)
title: Cranwell 'possible missile'

desc: Reported ghosts include a lady in white said to be a ballerina, a stagehand, a hooded figure and a lost child; an exorcism was reportedly held in 1969.
place: Lyceum Theatre, Heath Street, Crewe, Cheshire
title: Crewe Lyceum Theatre

desc: In April 2009 a CCTV clip appeared to show a glowing figure moving along a path towards the hall before vanishing, and the council brought in ghost specialists. Earls of Sefton are traditionally said to walk the grounds.
title: Croxteth Hall CCTV figure

desc: A caller told police they had seen an object with eight to ten lights around its edge. No explanation was recorded.
title: Crumlin ringed-light object

desc: Two young princes, legend says, were thrown from the bridge by Roger Mortimer, and their cries are heard on stormy nights.

sources.name: Paranormal Database

title: Crying princes at Farndon Bridge

desc: Phantom soldiers and the sounds of battle are said to occur around the 16 April anniversary, and a visitor in 1936 reportedly saw a dead Highlander by a grave mound.
title: Culloden battlefield

desc: A Llandudno couple reported a charcoal-coloured triangular craft over Cwm Mountain, and the following month an egg-shaped object with a sphere suspended beneath it. No explanation was given.
title: Cwm Mountain charcoal triangle

desc: A ridge about three miles from Tregaron is called 'Cwys yr Ychain Bannog'. Tradition says it was made when two Bannog oxen dragged away the carcass of a huge reptile killed by local people in ancient times. Location is approximate.
place: ridge c. 3 miles from Tregaron, Ceredigion
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

sources.name: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

title: Cwys yr Ychain Bannog: furrow left by dragging a giant reptile

desc: Cyril John, 64, reported an orange-lit egg-shaped object about 4 ft long swinging in a 50-60 ft arc, with a silver-suited figure hanging about 40 ft up, for roughly 25 minutes. It is one of several silver-suited figure reports from the spring 1977 wave.
source: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave

sources.name: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave
Mysterious Universe — 19.05 MU Podcast (Welsh Triangle / Peter Paget, 10 Feb 2018)

title: Cyril John's swinging egg and suspended silver figure, Milford Haven

desc: The day after the Llangadog creamery sighting, a dairy driver reported a large black cat at the edge of woodland at Ffairfach, about ten miles from Llangadog.

sources.name: Spooky Isles

title: Dairy driver sees large black cat at Ffairfach

desc: Engineer Mike Dunne, 25, photographed a dark disc-shaped object hovering over houses near Bidston Hill before it vanished; dozens of others were said to have seen it. Slemen calls the hill a UFO 'window area'.

sources.name: Liverpool Echo (Tom Slemen)

title: Dark disc photographed over Bidston Hill

desc: A local man filmed 40 seconds of daylight video showing a small dark object hovering over the castle. It then sank slowly and disappeared behind the walls.
title: Dark object filmed over Caernarfon Castle

desc: Katie Moore, 29, and four friends reported an unlit dark shape in the sunset sky over Cardigan Bay at 10:40pm that vanished while being photographed, briefly reappeared and vanished again.
place: Morfa Farm caravan park, Llanrhystud, Ceredigion

sources.name: Cambrian News (11 Jul 2022)

title: Dark shape over Cardigan Bay from Llanrhystud

desc: Harvest workers near Llangeitho reportedly saw a 'toili' (phantom funeral) at midday in Llanbadarn Odwyn churchyard. A real funeral followed soon afterwards.
place: Llanbadarn Odwyn churchyard, near Llangeitho, Ceredigion
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

sources.name: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

title: Daylight phantom funeral at Llanbadarn Odwyn

desc: Thirteen-year-old Deborah (Debbie) Swan reported a silver, football-shaped object moving erratically by a hedgerow on the same day as Mark Marston's encounter.
source: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave

sources.name: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave
Higgypop — The Welsh X-Files
Mysterious Universe — 19.05 MU Podcast (Welsh Triangle / Peter Paget, 10 Feb 2018)

title: Debbie Swan's football-sized UFO, Herbrandston

desc: A forestry worker said spiked spheres grabbed him beside a hovering dome. Police recorded it as an assault; ground marks were found.
title: Robert Taylor, Dechmont Woods

desc: Two roe deer carcasses with injuries some experts said matched a big cat kill were sampled by Warwick University. DNA tests found only fox and deer.
title: Deer carcasses at Woodchester Park

desc: Two police constables followed a bright cross-shaped light by car for around 15 minutes and reported a second object joining it. The sighting was attributed to Venus.
source: Wikipedia – UFO sightings in the United Kingdom
title: Devon 'flying cross' police chase

desc: A Colwyn Bay couple camping at the abbey said a huge, silent diamond-shaped object hovered roughly 60 feet up. They described spotlights that lit the ruins like a stadium and red lights arranged in a cross.
title: Diamond-shaped craft over Valle Crucis Abbey

desc: A home help found a neighbour's dog, Peter, killed on a farm near Llangadog. He said he saw a huge black cat with a smaller cat, and police saw one silhouette running away.

sources.name: Spooky Isles

title: Dog killed, huge black cat and smaller cat seen near Llangadog

desc: Dorothy Cale, her 10-year-old son Daniel, Yvonne Andrews and Anne Berry reported a dome-shaped light about 5-6 ft across flashing four times above a hedge. It is cited as one of the earliest reports of the 1976-77 St Brides Bay wave. Location approximate (midpoint of the route).
place: Road between Broad Haven and Milford Haven, Pembrokeshire
source: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave

sources.name: Cambria Stories — The Pembrokeshire UFO wave
Mysterious Universe — 19.05 MU Podcast (Welsh Triangle / Peter Paget, 10 Feb 2018)

title: Dome-shaped light on the Broad Haven to Milford Haven road

desc: A servant ploughing at Gogoyan saw his master, John Evans, walking near him in the field one afternoon. Evans had been in Aberystwyth, over twenty miles away, all day and said the servant had seen 'only my spirit'. Ceredig Davies records this as a family story about his own grandfather.
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

sources.name: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

title: Double of a living man seen ploughing field, Gogoyan

desc: A fireball was reported travelling across Douglas Bay at night. No explanation was given in the report.
title: Douglas Bay fireball

desc: John Harries (d. 1839), physician, astrologer and 'dyn hysbys', reportedly told searchers where a murdered girl was buried under a tree with a bees' nest. He was then brought before the Llandovery magistrates and discharged. He was said to keep a chained, padlocked book of spells that he opened only once a year.
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

sources.name: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

title: Dr John Harries, the wizard of Cwrtycadno

desc: Visitors report whispers, apparitions, organ music, a phantom carriage and servants' voices in the kitchens.
title: Duckett's Grove

desc: A series of silent black triangle sightings over the Black Country between 2007 and 2011 earned the nickname 'Dudley Dorito'. No explanation was established.
source: Wikipedia – List of reported UFO sightings
title: Dudley 'Dorito' triangles

desc: Lucette, a governess said to have drowned herself after being deceived by an officer, is reported in a winding sheet, especially on Christmas Eve.
title: Dunkenhalgh governess Lucette

desc: Three white objects were reported over the east of the city. Russian Antonov An-30 survey aircraft were put forward as the likely cause.
source: Wikipedia – UFO sightings in the United Kingdom
title: East Glasgow three white objects

desc: Residents watched slow-moving lights for about an hour late in the evening. They were attributed to the Northern Lights.
title: East Hull slow lights

desc: A motorcyclist heading for Manchester in the early hours claimed two beings in ski-suit-like outfits stopped and spoke to him. No corroboration was recorded.
title: East Lancs Road roadside aliens

desc: During a 2009 BBC overnight filming, a microphone recorded about 20 minutes of unexplained voices that the presenter did not hear; no source was identified.
title: Edinburgh Vaults voices

desc: During the 1904-05 Welsh revival, preacher Mary Jones and many others reported balls and columns of light around Egryn Chapel and along the Dyffryn-Llanbedr road. Journalists from the Daily Mail, Daily Mirror and Daily News came to investigate, and a local police constable also reported a light he could not explain. Proposed causes include earth lights on the Mochras Fault, marsh gas and gorse fires.
title: Egryn lights and the Mary Jones revival

desc: During a Faenol Festival evening, a Llanfairpwll family and festival-goers watched 11 silent orange lights in small groups travel up the Strait, stop at the Britannia Bridge, turn towards Bangor and climb steeply away. The fireworks had not started yet, and the RAF reported no aircraft.
title: Eleven orange lights over the Menai Strait

desc: Former owner Elizabeth Warburton is seen walking through walls, alongside a Tudor-dressed man, a WWII officer and a grey-haired woman by the piano. Visitors report banging, crying children and footsteps.

sources.name: Haunted Rooms

title: Elizabeth Warburton of Stanley Palace

desc: West Yorkshire Police logged a possible UFO after officers and other witnesses watched a static cylindrical object with a white light at each end near the TV mast for several minutes. The CAA could not identify it as an aircraft.
title: Emley Moor mast police sighting

desc: Furniture moving, knocking and a gruff voice reported in a council house, investigated by the Society for Psychical Research.
title: Enfield poltergeist

mu.title: 27.16 - MU Podcast - The New Opium Wars
mu.excerpt: Show-notes links: This House is Haunted: The True Story of the Enfield Poltergeist — https://amzn.to/3y0tkOw

desc: During the NATO Exercise Mainbrace a silver disc was reported following a Meteor jet back towards RAF Topcliffe, and RAF aircraft later chased a sphere over the North Sea. The case was raised in Parliament; no explanation was given.
source: Wikipedia – UFO sightings in the United Kingdom
title: Exercise Mainbrace disc over RAF Topcliffe

desc: A police officer reported a large explosion accompanied by an intense white light over the town.

sources.name: Daily Post

title: Explosion and white light over Rhuddlan

desc: Around 5:30pm Richard Davis, his wife and two children were driving home from Brecon when the youngest son saw flashing lights moving at speed in the sky above the car. The family called it 'unnerving'.
place: A40 towards Tal-y-llyn, near Brecon, Powys

sources.name: Brecon & Radnor Express

title: Family sees flashing lights moving fast above car, A40 Tal-y-llyn

desc: A servant went missing near the Gors Goch bog and his fellow servant was tried for murder and acquitted. On a conjurer's advice, the family went to a set spot a year and a day later and found him dancing in a fairy ring. Pulled out, he believed only minutes had passed. The story was first published in 'Cymru' (May 1893) by D. Lledrod Davies.
place: Allt Ddu farm, between Pontrhydfendigaid and Tregaron (Cors Caron), Ceredigion
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

sources.name: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

title: Farm servant spends a year and a day with the fairies, Allt Ddu

desc: Reported spirits at the former coach house include a Cavalier, a young girl and a Victorian farrier in a leather apron. When a resident told the farrier to leave, he is said to have answered back and vanished. Guests also report drawers opening by themselves.
place: Trevor Arms, Marford Hill, Marford, Wrexham

sources.name: Spooky Isles
Daily Post

title: Farrier ghost at the Trevor Arms, Marford

desc: Legend says a man and his son were imprisoned here and the father killed the boy and then himself rather than starve; the pair are said to appear in the room where they died. The castle is now a hotel.

sources.name: HauntedPlaces.org

title: Father and son of Leasowe Castle

desc: A large fawn-coloured cat was reported at Strabane, one of several big cat reports from the town since 2004.
title: Fawn-coloured cat at Strabane

desc: A farmer testing a neighbour's big cat sightings caught a female puma in a cage trap. Experts judged her a tame former pet and she lived out her life at the Highland Wildlife Park.
title: Felicity the puma trapped at Cannich

desc: A woman walking three dogs with her partner saw a Labrador-sized brown or black cat with a feline tail, which ran off; she reported it to police. The Fen Tiger has been reported in the area for decades.
title: Fen Tiger seen behind Abbotsley golf club

desc: Around 2pm one day in August 1862, waggoners David Evans and Evan Lewis saw about fifty small, identically dressed figures walk up a hillside path. The figures danced in a circle, spiralled 'like a gimlet screw' and vanished into the ground, then reappeared once before vanishing again. Ceredig Davies interviewed both men.
place: Cwmdwr, opposite Maestwynog farm, Llanwrda–Lampeter road, Carmarthenshire
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

sources.name: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

title: Fifty little figures dance and vanish into hillside, Cwmdwr

desc: A local investigator reported five saucer-shaped objects in a row over the sea, then a flash and bang as an RAF aircraft passed. RAF Leeming said he had seen a heat-seeking flare.
title: Filey Brigg five saucers

desc: At 5.15pm a witness saw a shooting-star-like object with a burning tail, about the size of a military jet, apparently falling towards the ground.

sources.name: Daily Post (North Wales X-Files)

title: Fireball in the Ogwen Valley

desc: In the 1960s a bearded phantom fireman in a brass helmet was seen sitting on a ladder; the witness rang the alarm bell and quit soon after.
place: Old Fire Station (Chez Jules), Northgate Street, Chester

sources.name: Paranormal Database

title: Fireman Jack of the Old Fire Station

desc: Three men fishing saw a brown or tawny animal about the size of a golden retriever, which they thought was a puma. Another man and his son abandoned a barbecue at the same spot in May after seeing a similar cat.

sources.name: Daily Post

title: Fishermen meet tawny puma at Gimblet Rock

desc: A man in a flat cap and blue overalls is reported in the Construction Hall and an elderly woman near the kitchen. Staff have also described lights and doors operating by themselves and men in boiler suits vanishing.

sources.name: HauntedPlaces.org

title: Flat-capped worker at Cammell Laird

desc: A strangely two-dimensional soldier with sergeant's stripes, a thin moustache and a swagger stick rides trains from Birkenhead Central and steps off at James Street. A lollipop man told Slemen he saw it in the 1990s with other passengers.

sources.name: Liverpool Echo (Tom Slemen)

title: Flat WWI sergeant on the Birkenhead train

desc: A drowned sailor in blue, said to have been laid out in the inn before burial, floats about the building, sometimes just head and shoulders over a mist; he was also seen 'digging' in the churchyard.
place: Punch Bowl Inn and churchyard, Sefton

sources.name: Paranormal Database

title: Floating sailor of the Punch Bowl, Sefton

desc: Four hill walkers said a black animal, possibly a puma, stared at them for a couple of minutes before vanishing into gorse.

sources.name: Daily Post

title: Four walkers watched by cat on Moel Hiraddug

desc: Four trawler crew reported a flat, shiny round object hovering about 19 miles north-east of Fraserburgh, briefly tracked on the boat's radar before it vanished. No explanation was given.
title: Fraserburgh trawler radar disc

desc: A local reporter counted 16 fast white lights crossing the sky over two nights. RAF Kinloss reported no aircraft; satellites were suggested but considered unusual in that number.
title: Fyvie fast white lights

desc: An elderly woman is said to appear near seat B14 and walk through a wall.
place: Gaiety Theatre, Harris Promenade, Douglas, Isle of Man
title: Gaiety Theatre seat B14

desc: A young woman near the golf course said a black cat bigger than an Alsatian leapt out at her and fled when her dog barked, adding to late-1990s rumours of a Galloway Puma around Kirroughtree.
title: Galloway Puma springs at dog walker

desc: Legend from early in Elizabeth I's reign tells of a strange ship with lights and ghostly figures in its rigging running aground by the island in a storm with no one at the helm, followed by a confessed pirate haunted by his victims leaping from the cliffs. Folklore, as retold.
source: Bluestone — Scariest stories from haunted Pembrokeshire

sources.name: Bluestone — Scariest stories from haunted Pembrokeshire

title: Ghost ship at St Catherine's Island, Tenby

desc: A chapel seat is kept empty for a White Lady thought to be Janet Douglas, and legends tell of a hidden 'monster' and of Earl Beardie gambling with the Devil.
title: Glamis Castle legends

desc: In summer 1983 people saw amber oval lights, then a large H-shaped formation that released smaller lights before folding in on itself and vanishing. Researchers linked it to a wave of sightings over the Clwydian Range, Prestatyn, Meliden and Dyserth in 1985-86.

sources.name: Daily Post

desc: Legend says five saints sleep inside the Roman gold workings until Arthur returns. A curious woman, Gweno, who went to spy on them (or passed the limit while bathing at the well) was lost in the mine. desc: Tradition says the ground rose under St David as he preached at the Synod of Brefi in 519. A Bannog ox bellowed nine times and split Foelallt rock, and a spirit pulled down by night the church begun at Godregarth farm. A horn core said to be the ox's, identified as aurochs, was long kept at the church.
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

sources.name: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg
Discover Ceredigion

title: Llanddewi Brefi: rising hill, bellowing ox and church-moving spirit

title: Llandudno Easter-egg object

desc: A farmer out shooting saw a bright white light come down slowly. Soon afterwards a mother at her window saw three tall figures in silver-grey suits walking across a field as cows stampeded. A catalogue review rates the case weak and suggests firefighters in protective suits.

patrickgross.org UFO catalogue

title: Llanerchymedd silver figures in a field

sources.name: Daily Post

desc: At 2.35am a resident watched a large black cat with a tail several feet long cross a paddock about 100 yards away for a couple of minutes. Horses in the paddock seemed undisturbed.

desc: A dog walker thought he saw a lynx on the golf course, and three more people later came forward with similar accounts.

desc: A bright oblong object with a rounded end was reported hovering silently over the coast. No explanation was given.

sources.name: Spooky Isles

title: Man in black in room 6, Ye Olde King's Head

Daily Post

title: Murdered miller at Bidston Windmill

title: Nantclwyd y Dre White Lady

desc: A black triangular object with green lights was reported over the town. No explanation was given.
title: Northallerton black triangle

Daily Post

desc: Local tradition told to Ceredig Davies says Einion of Ystrad Caron, who built a bridge over the Teifi, vanished for many years among the fairies. He came back on the day his 'widow' was due to remarry and proved who he was by playing his harp. The same bridge was 'once noted for its witches': a farmer said a witch jumped onto his horse there until he drew her blood.
place: Pont Einion / Ystrad Caron, Tregaron, Ceredigion

title: Pont Einion: harpist returns after years among the fairies

desc: A farmer named Edwards near Llanafan bridge was reportedly troubled day and night by a spirit. It dropped stones down the chimney, threw ashes in his milk, threshed in the barn and pulled down his fence, until he asked it in God's name what it wanted. It was said to have shown him treasure hidden in a wall. The bridge was also said to be haunted, with a recent sighting at the time of writing (c.1911).
place: Pont Llanafan (Llanafan bridge), Ystwyth valley, Ceredigion
source: J. Ceredig Davies, Folk-Lore of West and Mid-Wales (1911), Project Gutenberg

title: Witches' Mill, Castletown – Gardner's museum and coven
place: Arbory Street, Castletown, Isle of Man
desc: The 1828 windmill (rebuilt after a fire in 1848) was bought in the early 1950s by Cecil Williamson, who opened a museum of folklore and witchcraft there; he later sold it to Gerald Gardner, founder of Wicca, who ran it as the Museum of Magic and Witchcraft until his death in 1964. His successor Monique Wilson later sold the museum and its exhibits. The mill was listed in 1985 and converted into homes around 2000. It stands near the reputed home of the 17th-century 'Arbory witch'.

title: Ffynnon Elian – the cursing well
desc: Edward Lhuyd recorded healing offerings for sick children here around 1699, but by the later 18th century St Elian's well had become notorious as a cursing well: for a fee a keeper 'entered' a victim's name (on slate or paper, or with pins in a cork) into the water, and charged more to remove it. An 1818 account mentions a man indicted at the Flint Assizes for extorting money by pretending to free someone from the well. The well structure was destroyed around 1829 but the practice persisted for decades; the spring has since been restored by its owner. The pin is now from the Coflein record (NPRN 32271).

title: Hellfire Caves, West Wycombe

Contemporary rumour spoke of devil-worship and black masses, but the most reliable account (Horace Walpole) describes 'rigorously pagan' revels to Bacchus and Venus. The Inner Temple lies beyond an underground 'River Styx', reputedly beneath St Lawrence's Church; the caves have been a tourist attraction since 1951.

title: St Mary's Old Church, Clophill – 1963 'Black Mass' desecration
desc: The 14th-century church was abandoned in 1848 when a new St Mary's was built in the village, and fell into ruin. title: Kyteler's House, Kilkenny – Ireland's first witchcraft trial
desc: In 1324 Bishop Richard de Ledrede of Ossory accused Dame Alice Kyteler and her associates of witchcraft and heresy, including denying Christ, sacrificing animals at crossroads to a demon lover called Robert (Robin Artisson) and bewitching her husbands. Her servant Petronilla de Meath was tortured, confessed, and was flogged and burned at the stake on 3 November 1324 – the first known execution for witchcraft in Ireland. Alice fled, possibly to England or Flanders, and vanishes from the record; her name lives on in Kyteler's Inn.

title: Highgate Cemetery – 'Highgate Vampire' and black-magic claims
desc: Letters to the Hampstead and Highgate Express in February 1970 about a 'grey figure' grew into a media frenzy; after ITV broadcast interviews on 13 March 1970 a crowd of would-be vampire hunters climbed into the locked cemetery the same night. On 1 August 1970 the charred, headless remains of a woman were found near the catacombs and police reportedly suspected black magic. In 1974 one of the self-styled hunters was jailed for damaging memorials and interfering with remains, while insisting Satanists were to blame. Folklorists treat the 'vampire' as a press-fuelled legend driven by a rivalry between two occultists.

desc: On Good Friday, 10 April 1612, friends of the Demdike family allegedly met at Malkin Tower, the home of Elizabeth Southerns ('Old Demdike'), supposedly to plot freeing jailed relatives by blowing up Lancaster Castle. Magistrate Roger Nowell treated it as a witches' sabbat, and it triggered the Pendle trials. The tower's site is unknown: Malkin Tower Farm at Blacko rests on a hollow called Mawkin Hole and old masonry, but it lies several miles from places named at the trial; the 2011 Lower Black Moss cottage and land near Newchurch are rival candidates. title: Meon Hill – 1945 'witchcraft murder'
desc: On 14 February 1945 an elderly farm labourer from Lower Quinton was found killed in a field called Hillground on the slopes of Meon Hill, pinned to the ground with a pitchfork and slashed with a hook. Chief Inspector Robert Fabian of Scotland Yard suspected the farmer he worked for, but there was not enough evidence; his 1945 reports make no mention of witchcraft, and the 'pagan rite' interpretation appeared in his writing only years later and was disputed by Gerald Gardner. It remains Warwickshire's oldest unsolved murder. The pin is now on the summit (approx).

desc: The Pendle accused were held in Lancaster Castle's gaol and tried at the Lancaster Assizes on 18–19 August 1612 before Sir Edward Bromley; the clerk Thomas Potts published the proceedings in 1613. Ten of the Pendle accused were convicted and hanged. At the same assizes the three Samlesbury women were acquitted when their young accuser admitted she had been coached by a Catholic priest.

title: St Andrew's Auld Kirk, North Berwick – 1590 witches' sabbat
desc: Accused people in the North Berwick trials (1590–92) confessed under torture, often in Edinburgh's Old Tolbooth, to meeting the Devil in the Auld Kirk on Halloween night 1590 to raise storms against James VI and his Danish bride. More than 70 people were implicated; Agnes Sampson was strangled and burned, and Dr John Fian was burned on Edinburgh's Castlehill. The affair shaped James's Daemonologie (1597). The kirk ruins stand by the harbour.

title: Hagley Wood – 'Bella in the Wych Elm'
desc: On 18 April 1943 four boys found a skull in a hollow wych elm in Hagley Wood; police recovered an almost complete female skeleton, with the hand bones found some distance away. The pathologist put her death in or before October 1941. In 1945 Margaret Murray suggested a 'Hand of Glory' ritual; spy theories followed, and graffiti asking 'Who put Bella/Luebella down the wych elm?' has appeared since 1944, later on the Hagley Obelisk. West Mercia Police closed a review in 2014; she has never been identified.

title: Love Street, Chester — said to be the city morgue c.1900
desc: Lead from Bryn: Love Street is said to have been Chester's city morgue around 1900. Not confirmed. Research on 2026-10-29 found no public mortuary on the street in the Medical Officer of Health reports (1904, 1908, 1910–35), Kelly's directories (1896, 1902), the Victoria County History or the c.1898 25-inch OS map. What was there: Forest House on Love Street held the city's Public Health office (and the Union offices) until autumn 1910 — the MOH report says patients' progress could be enquired about there, which may be how the 'morgue' memory arose. The only mortuaries named in the records are the isolation hospital's and the Overleigh Cemetery chapels; inquests were held at the Town Hall. Still to check: Chester Wiki 'Love Street' page and the Cheshire Observer.

title: Sandling Park "bat beast" and Saltwood lights
place: Sandling Road, Saltwood, near Hythe, Kent
desc: On 16 November 1963, four teenagers walking towards Sandling station reported a reddish-yellow light that dropped behind trees. They then saw a headless figure about 5 ft tall with bat-like wings, which vanished near the railway bridge. Days later, John McGoldrick reported flattened bracken and three huge footprints in a nearby wood, and Keith Croucher reported an oval light on 21 November. Coordinates are approximate.

place: Falmouth Bay (Pendennis Point to Rosemullion Head), Cornwall
desc: A long-necked sea creature was reported off Pendennis Point in 1975, and Tony 'Doc' Shiels named it Morgawr after his own claimed sighting in 1976, also producing photographs near Mawnan; the 'Mary F' photos sent to the Falmouth Packet are attributed to him. The episode is widely regarded as a Shiels hoax tied to his 'monster raising' alongside the Owlman. Coordinates approximate.

desc: Around 1899 Aleister Crowley took a flat at 67–69 Chancery Lane, where he and Allan Bennett performed Goetic evocations. Pin at no. 67 (approx).

desc: On the morning of Thursday 27 June (year not stated in the online report; c. 2019) inverted crosses, a pentacle and the name 'Azazel' – a fallen angel – were found daubed in emulsion on the front doors of St Mark's Anglican church. Police appealed for information; no arrest was reported.

desc: From 1907 the magical order A∴A∴, founded by Crowley and George Cecil Jones, used 124 Victoria Street as its headquarters and temple. Coordinates are for Victoria Street (approx).

title: Maggie Wall monument, Dunning
desc: A rough cairn-like monument about 6 m high, topped by a cross and painted 'Maggie Wall burnt here 1657 as a witch', stands about a mile west of Dunning. It is first recorded around 1800; no record of a Maggie Wall exists, and some historians think it a folly or cenotaph for the several Dunning women executed as witches. The inscription is repainted anonymously.

title: Allt-y-Rhiw – witch-bottle under a yew
desc: An 18th-century Buckley-ware jug, about a quarter filled with lead, was found buried at the foot of an old yew at Allt-y-Rhiw farmhouse near Llansilin. Amgueddfa Cymru interprets it as a witch-bottle used to seal or trap a troublesome spirit. Coordinates are for Llansilin (approx).

title: Auldearn – Isobel Gowdie's 1662 confessions
desc: Between 13 April and 27 May 1662, probably in the Auldearn tolbooth, Isobel Gowdie of Lochloy gave four extraordinary confessions: a pact with the Devil at Auldearn kirk, a coven of thirteen, shapeshifting into hares, flights to feast with the Queen of Elphame, and clay images to harm the laird's sons. Forty-one people were arrested in consequence. Her fate is unrecorded. Pin on the parish church.

title: Caxton Hall – Crowley's Rites of Eleusis
desc: In October–November 1910 Crowley staged the Rites of Eleusis, a series of public magical performances, at Caxton Hall; the press attacked them as blasphemous.

title: 36 Blythe Road – Golden Dawn 'Vault of the Adepts'
desc: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn kept its ritual Vault of the Adepts at 36 Blythe Road. In 1900 Crowley, acting for MacGregor Mathers, tried to seize it from the London lodge (the 'Battle of Blythe Road'); a court ruled for the lodge. Coordinates are for Blythe Road (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Aleister Crowley

title: St Bridget's Church, Dyserth – 1637 'sorcerer' accusations
desc: In 1638 witnesses in a Court of Arches pew dispute called a Dyserth parishioner a sorcerer, blaming him for bewitching two oxen at Easter 1637, a hog some twelve years earlier, and a neighbour's fatal illness. The claims were made to discredit him as a witness, and no witchcraft prosecution followed. Pin on the parish church.

title: Witches' Stone, Forres
desc: A stone by Victoria Road at the foot of Cluny Hill marks where, by tradition, a woman accused of witchcraft died after being rolled down the hill in a spiked barrel; its plaque says barrels came to rest and were then burned. Tradition also links it to witches who allegedly cursed King Duncan. The barrel story is legend rather than documented history.

title: Manordeifi – 1616–18 image-magic accusation
desc: Between 1616 and 1618 a woman of Manordeifi was accused of 'fetish' witchcraft (image magic). The outcome is unknown. Coordinates are community-level (approx).

title: Wildboarclough – Mary Baguley, hanged 1675
desc: Mary Baguley of Wildboarclough was charged in April 1675 with bewitching to death a Wincle schoolmaster who fell ill, coughed blood and died. She was convicted and hanged that year, one of the last witchcraft trials in England to end in execution. Coordinates are hamlet-level (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Mary Baguley

title: Swansea Devil – the 'cursed' statue facing St Mary's
desc: Local folklore says a rejected architect placed a three-foot devil ('Old Nick') on a building facing St Mary's Church when Blomfield's rebuilt church opened in 1896, prophesying it would burn – and the church was gutted in the 1941 Three Nights' Blitz. The fire was wartime bombing, and the revenge story is legend. The statue vanished in 1962, was found in a Gloucester garage in the 1980s and has been displayed at Swansea Museum since June 2019 (pin).

title: Pittenweem – the 1704–05 witch hunt and lynching
desc: In 1704 a teenage blacksmith's apprentice accused several Pittenweem women of bewitching him; they were held and tortured in the tolbooth. Janet Cornfoot escaped, was brought back from Leuchars and on 30 January 1705 was lynched by a mob at the harbour – stoned, swung from a ship's rope and crushed under a door weighted with stones. No one was ever tried; a 2012 proposal for a memorial was voted down. Pin at the harbour.

title: St Mary's Catholic Church, Great Yarmouth – satanic emblem on altar
desc: During Holy Week 2018 (the night of Tuesday 27 March) CCTV showed a young man lighting small fires inside the church, trying to burn an icon and leaving a satanist emblem on the altar; months earlier a satanic picture had been left at the foot of a cross. Norfolk Police arrested a 17-year-old, and the bishop re-dedicated the altar about two months later.

title: St Mary's Church, Akenham – the 'Devil's grave'
desc: A broken tombstone in this redundant medieval churchyard is known as the Devil's grave: legend says walking anticlockwise round the church thirteen times will summon him. The church was also the scene of the 1878 'Akenham burial case' over an unbaptised child, which went to the High Court and fed into the Burial Laws Amendment Act 1880.

desc: The Rosicrucian Order Crotona Fellowship built its wooden Ashrama Hall (1936) and the 'First Rosicrucian Theatre in England' (1938) near Christchurch. Gerald Gardner joined the group, and scholars suggest some members were the circle he later called the 'New Forest coven', into which he claimed initiation in 1939 – a founding story of Wicca. title: Lincoln Castle – Belvoir witches hanged 1619
desc: Margaret and Philippa Flower, former servants at Belvoir Castle accused of killing the Earl of Rutland's heirs by sorcery, were tried before judges Hobart and Bromley and hanged at Lincoln on 11 March 1619. Their mother Joan had died at Ancaster on the way to trial, reportedly choking on bread she had asked for as a test of innocence.

desc: Two late Welsh witchcraft cases were heard at Haverfordwest Castle: in 1693 a Loveston woman accused of several harms, and in 1699 a Haverfordwest woman accused of making sailors sick. The outcomes are not recorded.

A nearby business feared it was aimed at them. No explanation was found; coordinates are town-level (approx).

title: Heavitree gallows, Exeter – the Bideford witches hanged 1682
place: St Luke's Campus, Heavitree Road, Exeter
desc: Temperance Lloyd, Mary Trembles and Susannah Edwards of Bideford were convicted at the Exeter Assizes largely on hearsay and hanged at the Heavitree gallows on 25 August 1682 – often called the last executions for witchcraft in England. The gallows site is now a car park at the University of Exeter's St Luke's Campus; a plaque at Exeter Castle names them.

title: Smelt Monument, Castletown – Margaret Inequane burned 1617
place: Market Square, Castletown, Isle of Man
desc: In 1617 Margaret Inequane and her son John Cubon were burned at the stake for witchcraft beside the market cross in Castletown; lore says she was caught performing a crop-fertility charm. It is the only recorded Manx witchcraft execution – later cases went to church courts. A plaque on the Smelt Monument, which stands on the site, commemorates them.

title: Witches' Well, Castlehill, Edinburgh
desc: A small bronze fountain by John Duncan, commissioned by Patrick Geddes in 1894, commemorates people burned as witches in Edinburgh between 1479 and 1722, many on Castlehill – including Dr John Fian of the North Berwick trials. Its imagery of serpents and foxglove alludes to good and evil uses of knowledge.

title: Mistley Heath – burial of the Witchfinder General
desc: Matthew Hopkins began his witch-hunt in nearby Manningtree in March 1644; with John Stearne he drove the trials of 1645–47, including Chelmsford, where nineteen women were hanged. He died at Manningtree on 12 August 1647 and was buried the same day at St Mary's, Mistley Heath (the church has gone). Tradition says he owned the Thorn Inn at Mistley. Coordinates are village-level (approx).

title: Bricket Wood – Gardner's 'Witches' Cottage'
desc: In 1945 Gerald Gardner bought a plot at the Fiveacres naturist club and re-erected a 16th-century cottage there, decorated inside with magical sigils. From about 1946 it was the ritual space of the Bricket Wood coven, with Gardner as High Priest and 'Dafo' as High Priestess – the first Gardnerian Wicca coven. desc: A walker found a pentagram in a circle drawn in a white substance on secluded Dunsapie Hill, with eye-motif graffiti on nearby rocks; a local pagan shop owner suggested a winter-solstice rite using salt or ash. The year before, a concrete 'altar' and a metal plaque had been removed from Whinny Hill above St Margaret's Loch. Historic Environment Scotland treats damage in the scheduled park as heritage crime. title: Knowehead House, Islandmagee – the 1711 witch trial
desc: After Mary Dunbar suffered fits at Knowehead House in 1711, eight women – Janet Carson, Janet Latimer, Janet Main, Janet Millar, Margaret Mitchell, Catherine McCalmond, Janet Liston and Elizabeth Sellor – were tried at Carrickfergus in March 1711, Ireland's last witch trial. Records are lost, but they were probably sentenced to a year's imprisonment and the pillory. Pin on the house site.

title: Standedge Tunnel, Marsden – sheep's heads and painted symbols
desc: On 31 May 1980 workmen found two sheep's heads and strange painted symbols about 1.5 miles inside the disused canal tunnels; a police search found nothing more. In the mid-1980s explorers saw white painted symbols, including a pentagram, in the chamber known as 'The Cathedral'. A 2010s Huddersfield Examiner look-back found no evidence of actual rituals.

title: Wern Wen farm – hidden barn curse inscription
desc: During building recording by C.R. Archaeology, a carved inscription was found on a tie-beam of an early 19th-century barn at Wern Wen farm, deliberately hidden behind boards: 'MELLDIGEDIG + FYDDO + LLE + HWN + AMEN' – 'May this place be cursed. Amen'. It names no one; researchers suggest a departing tenant or disgruntled servant, and note the cursing well at Llanelian-yn-Rhos about five miles away. The 1845 tithe map lists the farm; coordinates are approximate (Llangystennin parish).

title: Samlesbury Hall – the 1612 Samlesbury witches
desc: Three Samlesbury women, one connected with the Southworths of Samlesbury Hall, were tried at Lancaster on 19 August 1612 after a 14-year-old relative accused them of witchcraft, including attending sabbats at Red Bank by the Ribble. All three were acquitted when she admitted she had been coached by a Jesuit priest; historians see the case as anti-Catholic propaganda. Pin on the hall.

desc: Janet Horne, an elderly woman accused of riding her lame daughter as a pony to the Devil to be shod, was convicted by the sheriff and burned in tar at Dornoch in June 1727 (some sources say 1722) – the last legal execution for witchcraft in the British Isles. Her daughter escaped. A stone in Littletown marks the traditional site.

title: Llanasa – 1656 and 1690 witchcraft accusations
desc: In 1655–56 a Llanasa woman (from Picton) was jailed after a mariner claimed she had appeared to him surrounded by lanterns and led him to an alehouse where he fainted; she was bailed and more than thirty neighbours certified she had never been suspected of witchcraft, and no further action is recorded. In 1690 a local labourer was accused of maiming cattle after a fortune teller's hint, but sixteen gentry vouched for him and the case was dropped. Coordinates are village-level (approx).

She was committed to gaol in 1657, escaped and was recaptured, and at the Flint Great Sessions on 28 September 1657 faced four indictments: the grand jury threw out two and a petty jury acquitted her on the others. title: Askeaton Hellfire Club
desc: The red-brick and stone clubhouse built around 1740 by the St Leger family stands, now ruined, within the bailey of Askeaton's Desmond castle on an island in the River Deel. A painting by James Worsdale shows the members – local gentry such as the Crokers of Ballingarde and Wyndham Quin of Adare – and the club had closed before 1800. Like other Irish Hellfire Clubs it was associated with drinking and gaming; devil-worship stories are lore. Pin on the castle.

title: Maxwellton Cross, Paisley – grave of the 1697 Paisley witches
desc: After the Bargarran 'possession' accusations, seven people were hanged and burned at Gallow Green, Paisley, in June 1697 – among the last mass executions for witchcraft in western Europe. Their remains were buried at the Maxwellton Cross crossroads, and a horseshoe was later set in the road to guard against a curse they had reputedly laid on the town. A plaque now marks the spot in the junction.

title: Gloddaeth Hall – the backwards charm of 1594
desc: A charm written backwards – taken as proof of harmful intent – was found at Gloddaeth, home of the justice Thomas Mostyn, and gossip tied it to the healer Gwen ferch Ellis, supposedly hired by a woman who had quarrelled with him. She was convicted and hanged at Denbigh in October 1594, the first person executed for witchcraft in Wales. The charm itself was never produced in evidence.

title: Gallows Hill, Spital Boughton, Chester – 1656 witch hangings
desc: Chester's gallows stood on Gallows Hill (Barrel Well Hill) by the old leper hospital at Spital Boughton. Three Cheshire women were hanged at Boughton for witchcraft on 17 October 1654, and three more – Ellen Beach, Anne Osboston and Anne Thornton – on 15 October 1656, all maintaining their innocence. The site also has a memorial to the Catholic martyr John Plessington (1679). Coordinates approximate.

title: Kewlake Lane, Cadnam – ewe impaled with hay cross
desc: On 2 January 2020 a ewe was found stabbed to death (eight knife wounds) beside a pitchfork, with an upside-down cross made of hay on its fleece – part of the New Forest series that began with pentagram-marked sheep and the Bramshaw church graffiti in November 2019. Three more sheep were found dead on 16–20 January. A Winchester man arrested later that month was released without charge.

title: St Mary's Church, Bottesford – the 'sorcerye' tomb
desc: The monument to Francis Manners, 6th Earl of Rutland, records that his two sons 'died in their infancy by wicked practise and sorcerye' – believed to be the only English tomb naming witchcraft as a cause of death. The Belvoir Castle servants Joan Flower and her daughters were blamed: Joan died on the way to trial, and Margaret and Philippa Flower were hanged at Lincoln on 11 March 1619.

title: Chalice Orchard, Glastonbury – Dion Fortune's sanctuary
desc: In 1924 the occultist Dion Fortune's group acquired an old orchard at the foot of Glastonbury Tor, adding a hut, veranda and chalets; it served as a summer guest house and lecture centre, and from 1931 as the Society of the Inner Light's 'Sanctuary'. Fortune died in January 1946 and is buried in Glastonbury. Coordinates approximate (Wellhouse Lane area).

title: Montgomery – 1579 enchanted apple case
desc: In 1579 a group of men at Montgomery were accused of enchanting an apple and a powder to make a woman leave with one of them. The outcome is not recorded. Coordinates are town-level (approx).
